By '10 the term was already being self-applied by some far-right thinkers that had been involved in NRx and New Right thought since the early 2000s.

Paul Gottfried, the same person that coined paleoconservative in the 80s, coined "alternative right" around '08 to refer to paleoconservativism. It gradually became a big-tent term to include the various forms of neo-reactionary (NRx) right-wing thought that had been forming, culminating in fully robust far-right ideologies on places like LessWrong, and was colloquially shortened to "alt-right". Other influences include the European "New Right", and its embrace of ethno-nationalism.

What is NRx? The intellectual cousin of the alt-right. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Enlightenment (worth reading in its entirety)

A brief overview of alt-right, not completely without its flaws but overall decent introduction: http://www.breitbart.com/tech/2016/03/29/an-establishment-conservatives-guide-to-the-alt-right/

Despite its initial self-application years back, because of it becoming fairly mainstream, many that could be correctly described as alt-right now seem to disavow the label. In other words, Andrew Marantz of The New Yorker was actually correct when he points out that the label is kind of like "'snob' or 'hipster,' that is often disavowed by people who exemplify it.

One part the wiki gets right about the alt-right: "It has been said to include elements of white nationalism, white supremacism, antisemitism, right-wing populism, nativism and the neoreactionary movement. Andrew Marantz includes "neo-monarchists, masculinists, conspiracists, belligerent nihilists" Newsday columnist Cathy Young noted the alt-right's strong opposition to both legal and illegal immigration and its hard-line stance on the European migrant crisis. Robert Tracinski of The Federalist has written that the alt-right opposes miscegenation and advocates collectivism as well as tribalism.

The important thing to understand is that it is functionally a big-tent term. It has more centralized and coordinated elements like with what Richard Spencer is trying to do, as well as highly decentralized elements that arose and continue organically from places like 8chan (and LessWrong in the early days). As such it is mistake to classify the alt-right as a political philosophy, when it is more a set of political trends which includes political and social action.

If you are more interested in robust political philosophies that overlap with and influence the more sophisticated elements of the alt-right, than look into the various NRx philosophies.
